source: Li, Deng, Li, Li (2026) Spend Less, Reason Better: Budget-Aware Value Tree Search for LLM Agents
finding: A training-free value tree (BAVT) with a prompted step-level value beat budget-matched majority voting on four multi-hop QA sets, with a reasoning model (GPT-OSS-20B) and an instruct model (Qwen3-30B-A3B). The baseline spent the same budget in tool calls and tokens.
numbers: Low budget (5 calls) BAVT matched or beat the baseline at High (20 calls). OSS-20B baseline average EM rose 0.194 to 0.334 with budget. 2Wiki: BAVT 0.37 EM at Low vs baseline 0.38 at High. Bamboogle Low: 0.31 to 0.49 EM.
quote: BAVT operating under strict low-budget constraints surpasses baseline performance at 4x the resource allocation
limits: Multi-hop QA with a search tool (answers are exact-match checkable, but the value signal is the model's own). One 20B reasoning model, not o-series or Claude. Baseline is plain trajectory voting, not a stronger search. Author-run, no seeds or CIs seen in text.
agent_relevance: Best new evidence that a tree with a prompted value can beat equal-budget voting on a reasoning model. Supports gap 1 only for tool-using QA, not for pure thinking tasks.

source: Li et al. (2026) BAVT ablation (Table 1, OSS-20B, Middle budget)
finding: Tree structure alone hurts. Random expansion in a tree is worse than plain parallel sampling. The value signal gives the gain, and the budget-conditioned selection adds more.
numbers: Average EM over 4 sets: parallel baseline 0.268; tree with random expansion 0.215; tree plus step value 0.309; full BAVT 0.388.
quote: simply organizing the reasoning process into a search tree without intelligent guidance actively degrades performance
limits: Single model, single budget tier, EM on 4 QA sets. Row labels in the PDF text were garbled; values paired with the text of section 4.3.
agent_relevance: A tree without a good judge is worse than no tree (-0.053 EM). Supports G2/G5: branch only when the judge is trusted. Exploit-late scheduling adds +0.079.

source: Wang, Zhu, Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling: Efficiency Limits and Linguistic Signals
finding: On R1-distilled reasoning models, training-free and verifier-free scaling methods (PlanSearch, mixture of agents, best-of-N, sequential revisions, combined parallel+sequential, prover-verifier game) mostly under-perform plain majority voting. Non-reasoning models gain more from external search but stay capped.
numbers: Models: R1-Distill-Llama-70B, -Qwen-32B, -Qwen-14B, -Llama-8B, -Qwen-7B, QwQ-32B-Preview. Benchmarks include GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench. Almost all methods below majority vote for Llama-70B and Qwen-32B (Figure 4; exact values only in plots).
quote: for reasoning-optimized models, the most compute-efficient strategy is to prioritize sample diversity over search complexity
limits: Verifiers are the same LLM (prompted). Distilled models, not o-series or Claude thinking. No ToT or MCTS arm; PlanSearch is the nearest search method. Exact numbers are in plots I could not read from text.
agent_relevance: For reasoning models with a prompted judge, default to sample-and-vote. Supports the guardrail not to branch by default. Authors: prioritise sample diversity over search complexity.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Extending one thinking trace with 'Wait' first helps then hurts. Splitting the same thinking-token budget into several independent traces and taking the most consistent answer does better.
numbers: GSM8K, R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: 'Wait and think more' to 16000 tokens cut accuracy 11.8%; parallel thinking at the same budget raised it 10.1%. Accuracy fell 87.3% to 70.3% as average thinking went 1100 to 15980 tokens (one model, Figure 2a). At a 16K budget parallel thinking gave about 22% and 47% higher accuracy than 'Wait' and exact-thinking budget control.
limits: Math benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME-class), distilled R1 models. This is parallel vs sequential, not tree search. Selection uses the model's own likelihood.
agent_relevance: Depth in one chain has a ceiling; width at equal tokens is the safer use of budget. Cap chain length before branching.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models
finding: For QwQ, R1-Distill and LIMO, longer chains and repeated self-revision do not raise accuracy reliably. Parallel sampling gives better coverage and scales better at the same tokens. The paper classes tree search as parallel scaling guided by a signal.
numbers: Successful-revision rate (wrong to right) always below 10%. For QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5B the wrong-to-right rate was lower than right-to-wrong. Model keeps its original answer in over 70% of cases. Coverage compared on AIME: 40 revision steps vs 10 parallel samples. Their Shortest Majority Vote improves majority vote.
limits: Math (AIME-class) only, open reasoning models. No tree arm tested. Cites Chen for the rule that feedback accuracy must exceed 90% for revision to help.
agent_relevance: Self-judging revision is weak for reasoning models too, so a tree whose value comes from the same model inherits this. A length-aware vote (shorter chains win ties) is a cheap select operator.

source: Sharma and Chopra (2025) The Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Voting Beats Parallel Self-Consistency at Matched Compute
finding: Counter-evidence: at matched tokens, chains that refine earlier chains beat independent chains in most configurations on five open models including GPT-OSS-20B/120B and Qwen3-235B.
numbers: Sequential won 43 of 45 configurations (95.6%). Best gain 46.7 points: Qwen3-235B AIME-2025 with 6 chains, 76.7% vs 30.0%. GPQA-Diamond gains 11-14.6 points. Each chain capped at 4096 tokens; 6 chains = 24,576 tokens in both arms.
limits: The 4096-token cap per chain likely truncates parallel reasoning traces and favours sequential (my reading, not tested by authors). About 30 questions per AIME set, so wide error. No tree arm. Not peer-reviewed in my read.
agent_relevance: Contradicts Zeng and Ghosal. The answer depends on per-chain token caps. Treat parallel vs sequential as unsettled; test with uncapped chains before fixing S6.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS)
finding: A tree that decides at each node whether to branch wider (new sample) or go deeper (refine a scored child) beat repeated sampling and standard MCTS on code tasks, but not on ARC-AGI, where repeated sampling was best at budget 128.
numbers: Budget 128 generations, 3 runs. LiveCodeBench GPT-4o: repeated sampling 37.8, AB-MCTS-A (Gaussian) 39.1, standard MCTS 36.7. CodeContest GPT-4o: 37.9 vs AB-MCTS-M 40.6. ARC-AGI GPT-4o Pass@2: repeated sampling 15.0, AB-MCTS-A (Beta) 14.0, AB-MCTS-M 12.3, standard MCTS 9.0, sequential refinement 8.7. Average rank: AB-MCTS-M 2.3, repeated sampling 3.5.
quote: Our approach assumes the existence of a reliable score evaluator
limits: Scores come from code tests (external, sound). GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3, not reasoning models. Gains are 1-3 points with std of 1-2 on 3 runs. Authors note it needs a reliable score evaluator.
agent_relevance: Adaptive width/depth is a usable trigger rule when a sound check exists. Fixed-width MCTS is among the worst arms on ARC, a warning against fixed schedules. With only a prompted judge the conditions are not met.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) AB-MCTS at large budget on ARC-AGI (Figure 6, DeepSeek-V3, up to 512)
finding: At a larger budget, repeated sampling plateaus and AB-MCTS keeps improving, so the best method depends on budget.
numbers: Budget grew from 200 to 500 generations: AB-MCTS rose substantially while repeated sampling began to plateau; standard MCTS kept improving but stayed well below AB-MCTS (exact values only in the figure).
limits: ARC-AGI pass@2 with exact-match grader (sound). One model. Numbers not in text.
agent_relevance: Search can overtake sampling only after sampling saturates; at small budgets sampling wins. Gate branching on budget and on the observed plateau of sampling.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Step-judging is hard. Prompted general models and PRMs identify the first wrong step far less well than a final-answer check, and the gap widens on harder problems. A reasoning-specialised judge is much better.
numbers: 3,400 cases with expert-marked first error. F1 on first-error step, average over GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o 61.9 (chart values); QwQ-32B-Preview is competitive with GPT-4o and below o1-mini; open PRMs lower. In OlympiadBench 32.2% of solutions with correct final answers still contain a process error.
limits: Math only; the judge here critiques finished solutions, not partial states inside a live search. o1-mini and GPT-4o are 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gives a per-task judge accuracy range: grade-school math judged well, olympiad math poorly. A correct final answer does not prove sound steps, so a tree can reward flawed paths.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an outside signal the model cannot tell right from wrong, so self-judging lowers or keeps accuracy. With oracle labels correction helps a lot, which shows the gain depends on the judge.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 standard, 75.1 / 74.7 after 1 / 2 self-correction rounds. CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 / 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 / 89.0. Oracle-label table: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3 and GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5 as best I can pair the garbled rows; HotpotQA GPT-4 49 to 59.
limits: 2023 models and one feedback prompt. RL-trained reasoning models may differ (Zeng still finds low revision success). Oracle table was column-garbled; read the oracle figures as approximate.
agent_relevance: A judge with no ground truth can be a coin flip. Measure judge accuracy against a small labelled set first. If no check exists, do not branch on that judge.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert reviewers rated LLM ideas as more novel than human expert ideas. The LLM pipeline was overgenerate-and-rerank (flat), not a tree. Human reranking added a little.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews. Novelty (1-10): human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81. Idea-level tests (N=49): AI novelty 5.62 p=0.03; AI+rerank 5.78 p<0.01. Feasibility slightly lower for AI. Format standardised across conditions before blind review.
quote: AI ideas are judged as significantly more novel than human ideas (p < 0.05)
limits: NLP prompt-based research ideas, one agent (Claude-3.5-Sonnet), seven topics. Not length-normalised in the main score. Novelty is rated on the write-up, not tested by execution.
agent_relevance: First human-rated novelty gain for scaled LLM ideation, but from sample-and-rank, not from a tree. This is the baseline an idea tree must beat. No tree vs sample-and-rank arm exists in sources I opened.

source: Si et al. (2024) LLM judges of ideas (Table 11) and diversity (section 7.1)
finding: LLM evaluators of idea quality are near chance against average human review scores, and the generator saturates in diversity: sampling more does not give new ideas.
numbers: Accuracy on top vs bottom 25%: Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker 53.3%, GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3%; human inter-reviewer 56.1%; NeurIPS 2021 66.0%; ICLR 2024 71.9%. Of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 were non-duplicate (cosine above 0.8 on MiniLM).
limits: Idea-quality labels are human review scores of the study's own ideas; dedup threshold chosen by hand. Single domain and model.
agent_relevance: A prompted judge cannot rank ideas well, so an idea tree scored by a prompted judge prunes near chance. Also breadth saturates by duplication, one reason b above 3 may stop helping (gap 10). Dedup before scoring.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2024) Thought of Search: iteration counts and caveats
finding: GPT-4 wrote the successor and goal-test code for four domains after few corrections, then plain BFS/DFS solved whole datasets. Effort was 1 to 3 chat rounds per component.
numbers: Mean interactions: 24 game 1.2 (successor) and 1 (goal); mini crosswords 2.4 and 1.4; Blocksworld 2.8 and 1; PrOntoQA 1.6 and 1. 24 game 1361 of 1362 solved, 1.92-6.83s total. 20 of 20 crosswords. 502 of 502 Blocksworld. 4000 of 4000 PrOntoQA. LLM-in-loop Blocksworld estimate: about 14 days and over $1000.
limits: Crosswords assume 10 candidate answers per clue including the right one, which removes the hard LLM step. Blocksworld instances only 4-5 blocks. Human fixes counted as extra rounds. All four domains are fully observable, deterministic and rule-defined.
agent_relevance: Strong where a task has rules. Gives a cheap formalisability test: can a model write a correct successor and goal test in about 3 rounds against a few labelled cases? If not, skip code search (gap 6).

source: Dainese et al. (2024) Generating Code World Models with LLMs Guided by MCTS (GIF-MCTS)
finding: Code written by the model as a world model works for rule-bound environments, but the authors state it needs deterministic, fully observable settings and a clear text description.
numbers: APPS Competition split strict accuracy, Llama 3 70B, pass@20: zero-shot CoT 23.2, WorldCoder 25.1, GIF-MCTS 28.3 (rows paired by order in extracted text). CWMB: 18 RL environments. Code-model accuracy is always above normalised return, so a nearly right model can still plan badly.
limits: Limitations section: stochastic and partially observed environments leave verification open (no set result for a given input).
agent_relevance: Partial answer for gap 6: formalisation fails when outputs are stochastic or hidden, because no unit check exists. Detector: no deterministic test oracle means do not formalise.

source: Besta et al. (2024) Graph of Thoughts: evidence on decomposition vs search
finding: The GoT paper credits decomposition and easier merging for the gain, and tested only ChatGPT-3.5 (Llama-2 was worse and slower). It has no arm that does split-sort-merge without scoring or refinement.
numbers: Sorting: GoT median error 61% lower than ToT at P=64 and 69% lower at P=128, only a negligible gain at P=32; cost over 31% lower. Text: combining or concatenating subresults is usually an easier task than solving large task instances from scratch.
limits: Own ToT variants (ToT, ToT2), not Yao's code. Only GPT-3.5. Tasks have exact scorers. No ablation splitting decomposition, scoring and refinement. No human or reasoning-model test.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open but the authors' text supports the decomposition reading. Test: split, solve parts, merge by code (sorted-merge, set union/intersection) with no scoring. If that matches GoT, the graph is not needed.

source: Katz et al. (2024) cost comparison of LLM-in-the-loop search methods
finding: Methods that call the LLM at every expansion cost orders of magnitude more than code search, with no soundness guarantee.
numbers: Estimated cost at GPT-4-turbo prices (500 input tokens, 50 output per call): IO/CoT about $40, ReAct/ReWOO about $200, RAP about $14,000, LATS about $16,000 over the benchmark suites.
limits: Back-of-envelope with stated assumptions; input length ignored. Not measured in a live run.
agent_relevance: Cost is dominated by per-node LLM calls. Keep node judging to short, cheap or code calls.

source: Li et al. (2026) BAVT: instruct vs reasoning model scaling (section 4.2)
finding: An instruct model repeated the same failure under more parallel samples (baseline flat), while the reasoning model's baseline improved with budget. The tree helped the instruct model most.
numbers: Qwen3-30B instruct baseline average EM 0.289 (Low) to 0.293 (High); MuSiQue baseline flat at 0.12 EM, BAVT 0.21. OSS-20B baseline 0.194 to 0.334.
limits: The mode-collapse explanation is the authors' interpretation, not tested.
agent_relevance: Weak diversity in the generator is one reason width stops helping (gap 10). A tree can inject diversity by instruction; a reasoning model already has it.
